chapter_title: Concerning the Catechumen who found fault with the Elect: why he is angry.
chapter_note: This chapter is dominated by dialogue frame and pastoral/institutional exhortation (catechumen vs. elect/saints). Only small embedded fragments read like older doctrinal exposition (dual-essence anthropology; the divine element from the heights; the foreignness of the body/flesh of Sin). There is no sustained systematic correspondential mapping sequence here; the ‘core’ appears only as brief doctrinal clauses pressed into a disciplinary argument.

paragraphs.temporal_note: Formulaic hagiographic scene-setting (“Once again… my master, the apostle”).
Dialogue/question setup voiced by a catechumen; part of the compiler’s narrative apparatus rather than impersonal cosmological exposition.
Dialogue attribution (“our enlightener speaks…”), a classic Kephalaia frame marker.

Exhortation plus illustrative parable aimed at correcting behavior (“not constructive… do not…”). Natural imagery is used rhetorically (cosmos→audience), not as a closed cosmological mapping sequence.

paragraphs.core_text: They are gods as they stand firm in the image of the gods. The divinity that is planted in them came to them from the heights and [dw]elt in them.
paragraphs.removed_material: Removed the institutional application hook and praise framing (“This is also the case with the elect… They have done the will of the greatness.”) to isolate the doctrinal claim about an indwelling divinity from the heights.
paragraphs.temporal_note: Embedded doctrinal anthropology (divinity from the heights indwelling humans) inside an institutional identification of the Elect; the ‘elect’ framing reads later/applied, while the indwelling-divinity clause reads older and more impersonal.

paragraphs.core_text: they are established in a body that is not their own, hating the flesh of Sin that makes the other dwell in a foreign land. Due to this they shall be angry, and say and utter hard words to each others' faces.
paragraphs.removed_material: Removed the direct audience reassurance/exhortation (“However, do not you be troubled in your heart. You know, once and for all…”) to retain the causal mechanism: foreign body/flesh of Sin → anger.
paragraphs.temporal_note: Causal mechanism stated in cosmological-anthropological terms (foreign body; flesh of Sin as an agentive force) but embedded in second-person pastoral direction.

paragraphs.core_text: For you have known the mystery of the two essences, you have understood that what is good and what is evil dwell in every person.
paragraphs.removed_material: Removed surrounding imperatives and community-focused admonitions (“do not… do not… do not…”, plus evaluative comments about ‘constructive’ speech and ‘the saint’) to isolate the dual-essence doctrinal statement.
paragraphs.temporal_note: The ‘two essences’ doctrine is a compact cosmological principle presented as explanation; the surrounding rhetoric is disciplinary/pastoral, aimed at regulating speech and attitude toward the saints/elect.

Direct moral accusation and community-role justification (sins, lusts, teacher relationship). Even with mythic vocabulary (‘Cross of Light’), the paragraph is aimed at shaming/correcting the catechumen in the present setting.
Pure application-voice exhortation (“so that you may… Do not…”), entirely institutional/behavioral.
Narrative transition and reaction formula (“Then, when the apostle had uttered…”), part of the dialogic frame.

Catechumen’s contrition speech in the narrative frame (“Forgive me my sins…”). The explanatory phrase about ‘the old man’ is not presented as impersonal teaching but as a framed response within the story.
